newsitem.title: UK: Mark gyrations subside as EMU outlook in focus.
newsitem.headline: Mark gyrations subside as EMU outlook in focus.

text.p: Gyrations in the mark subsided on Tuesday as traders tried to decipher whether the French election results would lead to a broad economic and monetary union or to tensions between France and Germany.

France's opposition Socialist party, which looks set to wrest power from the ruling right-wing coalition in the second round of elections on June 1, backs EMU but wants more emphasis on growth and jobs. It also wants Italy and Spain to join EMU from the outset.

Concern that a left-wing government would dilute plans to cut the budget deficit initially boosted the mark against the franc on Monday. But the mark has given back ground on its European crosses amid speculation that a Socialist government would push for a broader EMU.

"Currencies outside the EU bloc like the dollar will be favoured until the uncertainty is out of the way but basically signs of a broad EMU will lead to peripheral markets being favoured over the core ones," said Adrian Cunningham, head of economics at Scottish Mutual Assurance in Glasgow.
Mark/French franc was quoted at 3.3757/62 at 1100 GMT against 3.3758/63 late Monday in Europe. Mark/lira was at 986.25/45 versus 985.95/6.25 while mark/peseta was unchanged at 84.43/44.
The mark could return to favour if Germany resists moves to a broader EMU membership, triggering concern about tensions between France and Germany, market watchers said.
"Mark/Paris is in a bit of a limbo at the moment, but anything politically destabilising out of France should be detrimental for (the franc)," said Paul Coughlin, a trader at Amex Bank.
That said, Germany's ability to keep countries like Italy and Spain out of the first wave of EMU is being reduced by the difficulties it faces in getting its own fiscal house in order.
German Posts and Telecommunications minister Wolfgang Boetsch said on Tuesday Bonn will sell off shares in Deutsche Telekom AG faster than planned in order to qualify for EMU.

"If the Maastricht criteria are not being strictly applied, it is difficult to see how European authorities will be able to limit membership of EMU to a narrow elite without a lot of dissent from those who are being excluded," said Cunningham at Scottish Mutual.
Moreover, signs of volatility in the mark crosses are likely to met with discreet central bank intervention from France, Italy and Spain, traders said.
These central banks have largely succeeded in keeping their currencies trading close to their parity against the mark in the European exchange rate mechanism.

The franc, for instance, has not traded more than one percent away from its ERM parity of 3.3539 per mark so far this year. It currently stands only about 0.6 percent weaker than this rate even after the larger-than-expected gains the Socialists made in Sunday's elections.
Mark/lira's current levels are not far off its central rate of 990 per mark.
"The French elections have had a knock-on effect on some of the high-yielding European currencies," said a trader at an Italian bank in London.
"But even if the mark goes back up, 990 (lire) will be the top and the Bank of Italy will probably come in to defend this level."
